patient_information: A 42-year-old German man with an unremarkable past medical history.
chief_complaint: A 6-day history of fever up to 40°C, arthralgias, and retro-orbital pain.
history_of_present_illness: A 42-year-old man presented to a hospital in Germany with a 6-day history of fever reaching 40°C (104°F), accompanied by arthralgias and retro-orbital pain. His symptoms started while traveling, and he presented the day after returning from a 10-week trip to Thailand.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient had just returned from a 10-week trip to Thailand. He spent two months on Little Koh Chang in the Andaman Sea, followed by five days in Hua Hin and five days in Bangkok. He did not take any antimalarial chemoprophylaxis, consistent with national recommendations for his travel itinerary.
vitals: On examination, his temperature was 39.1°C (102.4°F), blood pressure was 156/80 mmHg, pulse was 106 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 16 breaths per minute, and SpO2 was 95% on ambient air.
physical_exam: The physical examination was largely unremarkable. The patient was fully alert with a GCS of 15/15. There was no skin rash or lymphadenopathy. His chest was clear on auscultation, and the abdominal examination revealed no tenderness or organomegaly.
labs_and_diagnostics: Initial laboratory results showed thrombocytopenia of 81 x 10^9/L, an elevated CRP of 55 mg/L, and elevated liver enzymes (AST 62 U/L, ALT 106 U/L). A Dengue NS1 antigen test and a rapid diagnostic test for malaria were both negative. A subsequent thick blood film showed Plasmodium species trophozoites at a density of 920/μL. The species could not be identified on the thin film, but a species-specific PCR ultimately confirmed a mono-infection with P. knowlesi.
differential_diagnosis: Given the clinical syndrome and travel history, the primary differential diagnosis was dengue fever, although the duration of fever was long and the NS1 test was negative. Other considerations included Chikungunya, Zika, influenza, and acute HIV infection. Enteric fever was considered less likely. Malaria was a critical diagnosis to exclude, as a negative rapid diagnostic test is not sufficient to rule it out, especially for non-falciparum species.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient was admitted to the infectious diseases ward. Based on the positive blood film suspecting non-falciparum malaria, treatment was started with atovaquone/proguanil 250/100mg, four tablets once daily for three days. The patient recovered rapidly and was discharged on the fourth day.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis was Knowlesi malaria, caused by Plasmodium knowlesi. The diagnosis was confirmed by species-specific PCR after an initial thick blood film showed Plasmodium species trophozoites at 920/μL. This was despite a negative malaria rapid diagnostic test and initial difficulty in identifying the species by microscopy, which can be mistaken for P. malariae.
